sections.title: Basic Circuit Theory
sections.summary: Ohm's law (V = IR) and Kirchhoff's voltage law (KVL) — algebraic sum of voltages around any closed loop equals zero.

sections.title: The Atom
sections.summary: Atomic structure, valence vs. free electrons, ions, atomic number; silicon has Z = 14.

sections.title: Materials Used in Electronics
sections.summary: Conductors, insulators, semiconductors; energy bands (valence vs. conduction); covalent bonding via shared valence electrons.

sections.title: Current in Semiconductors
sections.summary: Electron current (conduction band) and hole current (valence band); silicon crystal sharing produces 8 effective valence electrons per atom.

sections.title: N-Type and P-Type Semiconductors
sections.summary: Pentavalent doping → N-type (electrons are majority carriers); trivalent doping → P-type (holes are majority carriers).

sections.title: The PN Junction
sections.summary: Depletion region, diffusion of majority carriers across the junction, barrier potential; forward bias narrows the depletion region, reverse bias widens it.

sections.title: The Diode
sections.summary: Diodes are normally operated in forward-bias or reverse-bias regions, not in reverse breakdown (except for special-purpose diodes like zeners).

sections.title: V-I Characteristic of a Diode
sections.summary: The V-I curve plots diode current vs. voltage across the diode, capturing forward, reverse, and breakdown behavior.

sections.title: Half-Wave Rectifier
sections.summary: A single diode that conducts only during one half of the input cycle, producing pulsating DC output.

sections.title: Power Supply Filters and Regulators
sections.summary: Filter capacitor smooths rectifier output by reducing ripple (V_r ≈ I_load / (f·C) — larger C means smaller ripple); regulator maintains a constant output voltage despite input or load changes.

sections.title: The Zener Diode
sections.summary: Designed to operate in the reverse-breakdown region as a voltage reference; forward-biased zener behaves like a normal silicon diode (~0.7 V drop).

sections.title: BJT Structure
sections.summary: Heavily doped emitter and lightly doped (physically larger) collector — terminals are NOT interchangeable despite being the same carrier type.

sections.title: BJT as Amplifier
sections.summary: Voltage gain of a common-emitter amplifier: A_v = R_C / r'_e.

questions.text: In a rectifier circuit, a smaller filter capacitor reduces the ripple.
questions.explanation: It's the opposite — a LARGER filter capacitor reduces ripple. Ripple voltage is approximately V_r ≈ I_load / (f · C), so larger capacitance means slower discharge between peaks and less voltage variation.

questions.text: The output voltage of a filtered rectifier always has some ripple voltage.
questions.explanation: A filter cannot completely eliminate ripple — only reduce it. Some residual ripple always remains because the capacitor must discharge slightly between charging cycles. Ripple can be minimized but never zeroed out.

questions.text: Reverse breakdown occurs when the reverse-bias voltage of a diode equals or exceeds the barrier potential of the pn junction of a diode.
questions.explanation: Reverse breakdown occurs at the BREAKDOWN voltage (V_BR), which is much greater than the barrier potential. The barrier potential (~0.7 V for silicon) is what must be overcome in FORWARD bias, not reverse.

questions.text: Diffusion is the movement of the holes (majority carriers) in the n-region across the pn junction and into the p region.
questions.explanation: Holes are majority carriers in the P-region, not the N-region. In the N-region, free electrons are the majority carriers. At the junction, electrons diffuse from N→P and holes diffuse from P→N.

questions.text: The diode in a half-wave rectifier conducts for half the input cycle.
questions.explanation: The diode is forward-biased and conducts during one half of the input AC cycle (typically the positive half), and reverse-biased during the other half. This is exactly why it's called 'half-wave.'

questions.text: A positive ion is a previously neutral atom that has lost a valence electron and has a net positive charge.
questions.explanation: When a neutral atom loses a valence electron, it has more protons than electrons, leaving a net positive charge. This is the textbook definition of a positive ion (cation).

questions.text: To reverse-bias a diode, the positive side of an external bias voltage is applied to the n region and the negative side to the p region.
questions.explanation: Reverse bias: (+) to cathode (N region), (–) to anode (P region). This pulls majority carriers away from the junction, widening the depletion region and blocking conduction (until breakdown).

questions.text: The voltage that appears across a zener diode when it is forward-biased is approximately 0.7 V, just like a rectifier diode.
questions.explanation: Forward-biased, a zener diode behaves identically to a regular silicon diode (~0.7 V drop). Its special voltage-regulating behavior occurs only in REVERSE breakdown, where it maintains the zener voltage V_Z.

questions.text: Hole current occurs at either the valence level or conduction level.
questions.explanation: Hole current occurs ONLY at the valence band level — it's the apparent motion of holes as valence electrons fill adjacent vacancies. Free electron current occurs at the conduction band level. Holes do not exist as carriers in the conduction band.

questions.text: A valence electron is an electron that has broken free of its parent atom.
questions.explanation: That definition describes a FREE electron. A valence electron is an electron in the outermost shell that is still bound (loosely) to its parent atom. A valence electron can become a free electron after absorbing enough energy.

questions.text: Covalent bonds are formed by the sharing of free electrons and holes with neighboring atoms.
questions.explanation: Covalent bonds form by sharing VALENCE electrons (not free electrons or holes) with neighboring atoms. Free electrons have already escaped the atom, and holes are absences of electrons — neither can participate in covalent bonding.

questions.text: Conductors such as copper have one valence electron.
questions.explanation: Copper, silver, and gold each have a single, loosely held valence electron that detaches easily to become a free electron. This is why these metals are excellent conductors of electricity.

questions.text: Insulators have essentially no free electrons and do not conduct current.
questions.explanation: Insulators have a very large energy gap between valence and conduction bands, so virtually no electrons gain enough energy to become free under normal conditions. With no charge carriers, no significant current flows.

questions.text: Two types of current in a diode are electron and hole.
questions.explanation: In any semiconductor (including diodes), current is carried by free electrons (conduction band) and holes (valence band). Across a forward-biased PN junction, electrons flow N→P and holes flow P→N — both contribute to total current.

questions.text: The depletion region for forward bias is much wider than for reverse bias.
questions.explanation: It's reversed — the depletion region is much NARROWER under forward bias and WIDER under reverse bias. Forward bias pushes majority carriers toward the junction (narrowing it); reverse bias pulls them away (widening it).

questions.text: The difference in doping levels of the collector and emitter on a BJT makes the two terminals interchangable except that holes will flow from emitter to collector instead of electrons.
questions.explanation: The collector and emitter are NOT interchangeable. The emitter is heavily doped, while the collector is lightly doped and physically larger to dissipate heat. Swapping them severely degrades β and the transistor's power-handling capability.

questions.text: The V-I characteristic curve shows the diode current as a function of voltage across the diode.
questions.explanation: The V-I curve plots diode current (I_D) on the y-axis vs. voltage across the diode (V_D) on the x-axis. It captures the diode's forward conduction, reverse blocking, and breakdown behaviors graphically.

questions.text: A pentavalent atom has three valence electrons.
questions.explanation: PENTA = 5, so a pentavalent atom has FIVE valence electrons (e.g., phosphorus, arsenic, antimony — used as N-type dopants). A TRIvalent atom has three valence electrons (e.g., boron, gallium — used as P-type dopants).

questions.text: Zener diodes are operated in the reverse-breakdown region.
questions.explanation: Zener diodes are specifically designed to operate in reverse breakdown, where they maintain a nearly constant voltage (V_Z) across a wide range of currents. This makes them ideal for voltage regulation.

questions.text: RC and r'e determine the voltage gain of half-wave rectifier.
questions.explanation: R_C and r'_e determine the voltage gain of a BJT AMPLIFIER, where A_v = R_C / r'_e. A half-wave rectifier doesn't have voltage gain in the amplifier sense — it just converts AC into pulsating DC.

questions.text: The majority carrier in an n-type semiconductor is the free electron.
questions.explanation: In N-type material, the pentavalent dopant donates extra free electrons, making them the majority carriers (and holes the minority carriers). In P-type material the opposite is true: holes are majority, electrons are minority.

questions.text: How does the voltage (V) in a circuit change if the resistance (R) is doubled while keeping the current (I) constant?
questions.explanation: From Ohm's law: V = I × R. With I held constant, V is directly proportional to R, so doubling R doubles V.

questions.text: The energy band in which free electrons exist is the
questions.explanation: Free electrons have absorbed enough energy to escape the valence band and exist in the conduction band, where they can drift under an applied electric field and produce electron current.

questions.text: What is the primary function of a filter in a power supply?
options: To convert AC into pulsating DC
To maintain a constant output voltage under varying conditions
To reduce the variation of the output voltage from a rectifier
To add a DC level to an AC voltage
questions.explanation: The filter smooths the pulsating DC output of the rectifier by reducing ripple. (Converting AC to pulsating DC is the rectifier's job; maintaining a constant output is the regulator's job.)

questions.text: The current in a semiconductor is produced by
questions.explanation: Semiconductors have two charge carriers: free electrons (conduction band) and holes (valence band). Both contribute to total current — this is the defining feature distinguishing semiconductors from pure conductors.

questions.text: A diode is normally operated in
questions.explanation: Standard rectifier diodes are operated in either the forward-bias region (conducting) or the reverse-bias region (blocking). Reverse breakdown is normally avoided since it would destroy a rectifier diode (zeners are the special-case exception).

questions.text: Which component in the voltage regulation process is directly responsible for maintaining the output voltage to a constant level regardless of changes in input voltage or load conditions?
questions.explanation: The regulator maintains a constant output voltage despite variations in input voltage or load. (Transformer steps voltage; rectifier converts AC→pulsating DC; filter smooths ripple.)

questions.text: Each atom in a silicon crystal has
options: eight valence electrons, four of its own and four shared
no valence electrons because all are shared with other atoms
questions.explanation: An isolated silicon atom has 4 valence electrons. In a crystal lattice, each atom shares one electron with each of its 4 neighbors via covalent bonding, giving each atom an effective 8 valence electrons (4 of its own + 4 shared).

questions.text: Given a circuit with three voltage sources of 12V, -4V, and 9V arranged in a closed loop with a prescribed direction, using Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL), what should be the algebraic sum of voltages around this loop?
questions.explanation: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law states that the algebraic sum of all voltages around any closed loop equals zero — always, regardless of the individual source values. This is a direct consequence of energy conservation.

questions.text: What effect does forward bias have on the depletion region in a p-n junction semiconductor?
options: It inverses the polarity of the region.
questions.explanation: Forward bias pushes majority carriers toward the junction, neutralizing some of the depletion region's ions. This narrows the depletion region and reduces the barrier potential, allowing current to flow.

questions.text: The atomic number of silicon is
questions.explanation: Silicon (Si) has atomic number 14 — 14 protons and 14 electrons. Its electron configuration is 2-8-4: two in the inner shell, eight in the second, and four valence electrons in the outer shell.
